niche: a state port authority's crane replacement placed by the berth hours a faster cargo finish would have saved its fiscal year's large-vessel calls, where deep-draught ships leaving the river terminals sail only in the tidal window at the river bar; built from AIS berth segments, two terminal operating systems' crane logs, the pilot dispatch export and the bar's tide predictions
analyst_test: With every log conformed and every rule read, the easy route takes a fifth off each fiscal year 2026 large-vessel call's cargo work and credits that time to its terminal, placing the cranes at Saltworks, which logged the most large-vessel cargo hours; but a deep-draught ship leaving a Salt River berth sails only in the tidal window at Salt Point, so the berth time saved there is the change in the window the ship would have made, almost nothing at Saltworks where ships finish hours before their window and a whole tide at Millrace where the old cranes make them miss it, and the cranes belong at Millrace.
domain_test: Port berth planning under tidal access: the berth time a faster crane set saves is the change in when a ship can sail, the cargo time cut at a deep-water berth and the change in the tide it makes at a tidal river berth; with another field's nouns there is no channel draught or tide and the counterfactual departure the call turns on does not exist.

spine.grain: crane x vessel visit x hour

world.geography: United States (a fictional East Coast port, Ternmouth)
world.org_type: state port authority owning and operating six container terminals

driver: A job's completion is released only inside windows a schedule outside the job fixes, so shortening the job's own work saves time only where it brings the release forward to an earlier window: a job already waiting for its window saves nothing and one that just missed a window saves a whole cycle, so crediting every job with the time cut from its own work picks the wrong place.
driver_concrete: A deep-draught ship leaving a Salt River berth sails only in the tidal window at Salt Point, so the replacement cranes' faster cargo finish shortens its stay only where the ship would then have been ready for an earlier window: almost never at Saltworks, where ships finish hours before their window, and by a whole tide at Millrace, where the old cranes make ships miss it; crediting every fiscal year 2026 large-vessel call with the fifth of its cargo time the cranes would cut places them at Saltworks instead of Millrace.
stump: The default path credits every large-vessel call with a fifth of its cargo work and places the cranes at Saltworks, because it never asks whether a ship leaving a river berth could have sailed any earlier than its tide allowed.

differentiation.task92: task92 values a capped service only on the days each candidate receives it, days stated nowhere and recovered from history; here the windows are filed tidal windows at the river bar and the quantity is a ship's counterfactual departure, so a faster finish saves nothing while the ship still waits for the same tide and a whole cycle where it would have made the one it missed.
differentiation.task472: architecture 1 counted the berth hours breakdowns cost through the slowest of a call's parallel crane runs; architecture 2 has no breakdowns and no crane runs in its decisive step: the cargo work is cut uniformly and the saving is gated by a release window outside the work.

lineage.layer2_pattern: own:slowest-section counterfactual for a stoppage on one of several parallel crane sections
lineage.driver: A job worked by several parallel streams that each keep their own share of the work is finished only when its slowest stream is, so a stoppage on one stream costs the job only what it pushes that stream past the others' finish; summing the stopped time, or charging each stoppage a share of the pooled capacity, picks the wrong place.
lineage.niche: a state port authority's container-crane replacement, judged on the berth time quay-crane breakdowns cost large vessels, built from AIS berth segments, two terminal operating systems' crane logs and two maintenance systems' work orders
lineage.stump: The default path charges every hour a crane working a large vessel spent broken down to that vessel's stay and recommends the terminal with the most such hours, because it never asks whether the stopped crane's run of bays was the one the vessel was waiting on.
lineage.fate: spent at stage 4 on 2026-10-20: both scored readers landed the call (score_reader exit 1 on each), reading rule 2.4's 'taken together, lengthened its stay alongside' as the slowest-crane counterfactual, the whole-hour terminal totals confirming it; re-rooted the same day
